editorial.headline: Other Tuber Farming, Without the Bali Moratorium Trap
editorial.standfirst: A broad farming category for sweet potato, taro, porang and similar tubers, open across business scales and available to full foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
This activity is the farming of tubers that sit outside the better-known main categories: sweet potato, taro, ganyong, irut, gembili, iles-iles, porang, and similar crops. The scope is not just the moment of harvest. It covers the agricultural chain when it is carried out as one integrated activity: preparing the land, planting, maintaining the crop, harvesting, and handling post-harvest work. In plain English, this is a working farm code for growers whose business is rooted in miscellaneous tuber cultivation, including crops that may later become food, starch, or upstream agricultural supply.

The record also reaches into related growing activity where the work is still agricultural in character. It includes nursery and seed activities for other vegetable plants, except beet seed, and it captures integrated land preparation, planting, maintenance, harvesting, and post-harvest work for vegetables, fruits, and mixed tubers harvested more than once, as well as other vegetable farming. That makes the scope wider than a single crop label. A founder should read it as an agricultural production category, not as a trading, processing, export, or retail category; the source record gives farming activities, not downstream commercial permissions.

On scale, the code is unusually broad: it is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the same activity can be used by very small operators and by larger agricultural ventures, provided the registered activity genuinely matches the farming work described in the scope. The cleanest reading is practical rather than decorative: if the business is cultivating these crops and the land preparation, planting, care, harvest, and post-harvest steps form one operational chain, this is the field of activity the record describes.

For foreign ownership, the national position is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership shown in the record is 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The Bali picture is also clear, and here it is not the negative one: the record is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The reason given is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not caught by Bali province's island-wide, permanent block on Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: this activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, and the Bali status in the record is not blocked by the moratorium.
